topic: How Computers Work (CPU, RAM, storage, GPU, bottleneck prediction)
objective: Describe what a CPU, RAM, storage and GPU each do, and why the difference matters; explain why a program must be loaded into RAM before it can run; predict which component is the bottleneck for a given workload.
current_strength: Strong. Accurate fetch-decode-execute and CPU/RAM/storage/GPU model, effective worked example (compute-bound render misdiagnosed as a RAM problem), hands-on system-monitor activity, and a challenge that pays off on Day 20. All three objectives are directly tested by the quiz.
identified_gap: The hardware model omits the NPU (Neural Processing Unit), a dedicated on-device AI accelerator now mainstream in Windows Copilot+ PCs and Apple Silicon Macs, and directly relevant to the day's own bottleneck-prediction objective — a learner running the day's own Task Manager exercise on modern hardware will now see an NPU meter the lesson gives no framework for.
research_finding: Microsoft's own official developer documentation confirms the NPU is a distinct, named hardware category (not a marketing term) purpose-built for AI inference, more power-efficient than CPU/GPU for that workload, rated in TOPS, and now directly visible in Windows Task Manager alongside CPU/GPU/Memory/Disk. The hardware category spans multiple vendors (Qualcomm, Intel, AMD), not one platform.
proposed_enhancement: Add 1-2 sentences to the end of the Core material segment's GPU paragraph introducing the NPU as a fifth hardware category increasingly relevant to the day's own 'predict the bottleneck' objective, plus an optional one-line addition to the Hands-on segment inviting learners with an NPU-equipped machine to check that meter too.
implementation_location: Core material segment (GPU paragraph, append); optional one-line addition to the Hands-on segment. No new timed segment.
estimated_time_impact: Negligible (~1 minute additional reading; no change to the 60-minute total)
assessment_impact: None proposed. Existing GPU-related quiz questions (q3, q4, q5) remain valid unchanged; no new question required for a P2 enrichment.
resource_impact: None. No new resource entry proposed; the two evidence sources are citations for the justification, not curriculum resource additions.

topic: Operating Systems (process vs. program, permissions, terminal)
objective: Explain what an operating system actually manages; distinguish a process from a program, and a file path from a file; use the terminal for basic navigation with confidence about what each command does.
current_strength: Strong. Accurate process/program/permission model, effective 'referee' and 'not a more-powerful mode' analogies, realistic file-not-found example, hands-on terminal task, all three objectives tested including a realistic permission-troubleshooting scenario.
identified_gap: No content gap identified. Secondary, non-content observation: the Microsoft Learn training-catalogue resource (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/) is a broad catalog root rather than a specific OS/file-system module, echoing a weak-resource pattern already flagged elsewhere in this project (e.g. M16.2's Day 23 EDTECH-001 finding). Not independently re-verified with a new source this session and not elevated to a day-level decision.
research_finding: None pursued — no genuine content gap was found, and researching a day with nothing wrong would be research for its own sake, which is out of scope.
resource_impact: Observation only (catalog-root resource) logged for a possible future, separately-scoped resource-verification pass. No replacement proposed or evidenced this session.

topic: Files, Data & Storage (format vs. extension, encoding, CSV/JSON/Markdown)
objective: Explain the difference between a file format and a file extension; choose an appropriate format for text, tabular, structured and media data; describe what encoding is and why it breaks things.
current_strength: Strong. Precise 'file = named byte sequence' framing, correctly and deliberately scoped to CSV/JSON/Markdown with a stated rationale tied to the rest of the curriculum, realistic LMS-import comma-bug example, hands-on CSV/JSON comparison, all objectives directly tested.
identified_gap: None identified. UTF-8-as-default, CSV/JSON dominance, and the encoding-mismatch failure mode are stable, non-time-sensitive facts.
research_finding: None pursued — no genuine gap found.
resource_impact: None. Both existing resources (MDN, Python official docs) are specific, official, and on-topic.

topic: Internet Fundamentals (IP, DNS, HTTP, HTTPS, status codes)
objective: Trace what happens between typing a URL and seeing a page; explain IP, DNS and HTTP in terms of the job each one does; read a URL and identify its parts.
current_strength: Strong. Clear protocol-role separation, realistic 401-misdiagnosis example paralleling Day 1's diagnostic-habit example, reusable status-code triage table, DevTools hands-on activity, all objectives directly tested including an applied-judgment question on 429 backoff behavior.
identified_gap: None material. HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 wire-level differences were considered and judged out of scope: they do not change what the stated objectives ask the learner to do (trace the lifecycle, explain each protocol's job, read a URL), so adding them would be interesting trivia rather than added capability.
research_finding: None pursued — no genuine gap found after the pedagogical audit.
resource_impact: None. Both existing resources (Cloudflare Learning Center, MDN) are specific, authoritative, and correctly scoped.
